category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: The myenteric plexus is specifically situated between the [___] and circular muscle layers of the gastrointestinal wall.
back:
● Longitudinal muscle layer.
● Extends from the esophagus to the anus.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: A patient presents with dysphagia and a "bird's beak" appearance on barium swallow. Pathophysiological studies likely reveal damage to the [___] in the lower esophageal wall.
back:
● Myenteric plexus (Auerbach’s plexus).
● Results in failure of Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) relaxation.
● Characterized as Achalasia.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Outline the primary motor influences exerted by the myenteric plexus upon stimulation.
back:
● Increased tonic contraction (tone).
● Increased intensity and rate of rhythmic contractions.
● Increased velocity of excitatory wave conduction (faster peristalsis).

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
coreConcept: Enteric Nervous System Division of Labor
front: Contrast the primary physiological roles of the myenteric plexus versus the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus.
back:
● Myenteric: Controls GI motility and muscle movement.
● Submucosal: Controls local secretion, absorption, and local blood flow within segments.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Identify the specific inhibitory neurotransmitters released by myenteric neurons to relax gastrointestinal sphincters.
back:
● Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP).
● Nitric Oxide (NO).

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Congenital absence of the myenteric plexus in a distal segment of the colon results in the clinical condition known as [___].
back:
● Hirschsprung’s disease (Megacolon).
● Characterized by severe constipation and proximal colonic distention.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
coreConcept: Myenteric Reflex and Law of the Gut
front: During the peristaltic reflex, the gut wall relaxes several centimeters downstream to allow food propulsion. This "receptive relaxation" is an integrated function of the [___].
back:
● Myenteric plexus.
● Part of the "Law of the Gut."
● Mediated by downstream inhibitory signals.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Explain why administration of atropine results in the depression of gastrointestinal peristalsis despite the presence of myogenic "slow waves."
back:
● Atropine paralyzes cholinergic (ACh) nerve endings.
● ACh from the myenteric plexus is essential for strong, effectual peristaltic contractions.
● Slow waves alone rarely trigger significant motor propulsion.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Distinguish between the effects of myenteric stimulation on the general gut wall versus the intestinal sphincters.
back:
● Gut Wall: Generally excitatory (increased tone/contraction).
● Sphincters: Often inhibitory (VIP/NO release) to facilitate forward food movement.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Provide the eponym used to refer to the myenteric nerve plexus.
back:
● Auerbach’s plexus.
● Contains over 100 million neurons (more than the spinal cord).

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: The [___] plexus, also known as Auerbach’s plexus, is primarily responsible for controlling gastrointestinal movements and motility.
back:
• Myenteric plexus
• Located between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers
• Extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: A newborn fails to pass meconium and exhibits a dilated colon. Biopsy reveals a congenital absence of the myenteric plexus. This condition leads to impaired motility because the myenteric plexus normally [___].
back:
• Controls GI motor activity
• Facilitates peristaltic waves
• Increases tonic contraction and the rhythmicity of the gut wall.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Explain how the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus regulates the internal environment of a specific gut segment.
back:
• Integrates sensory signals from the epithelium
• Controls local intestinal secretion and absorption
• Regulates local blood flow and submucosal muscle contraction.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Contrast the physiological roles of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses in a patient presenting with an overactive 'law of the gut' versus excessive mucosal secretion.
back:
• Myenteric: Controls peristaltic reflex and propulsion (Law of the Gut)
• Submucosal: Controls local mucosal secretion and absorptive responses to luminal stimuli.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Identify the specific inhibitory neurotransmitter often released by myenteric neurons to relax gastrointestinal sphincters like the pyloric sphincter.
back:
• Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP)
• Nitric Oxide (NO)
• These substances prevent obstruction of food movement between GI segments.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: While the myenteric plexus is situated between muscle layers, the [___] plexus is found within the submucosa to manage local secretion and blood flow.
back:
• Meissner's plexus (Submucosal plexus)
• Handles minute segment functions
• Integrates local sensory input from the gut wall.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: In a laboratory study, the myenteric plexus of a gut segment is stimulated. Predict the three primary effects on the smooth muscle's mechanical activity.
back:
• Increased tonic contraction (tone) of gut wall
• Increased intensity/rate of rhythmic contractions
• Increased velocity of excitatory wave conduction (rapid peristalsis).

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Describe the functional significance of inhibitory neurons within the myenteric plexus specifically regarding gastrointestinal sphincters.
back:
• Secrete inhibitory peptides (e.g., VIP)
• Relax the pyloric and ileocecal sphincters
• Facilitate forward movement of chyme into succeeding gut segments.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Distinguish between the myenteric and submucosal plexuses based on their anatomical location within the GI wall.
back:
• Myenteric (Auerbach’s): Between outer longitudinal and inner circular muscle layers
• Submucosal (Meissner’s): Within the submucosal layer of the gut wall.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Identify the total approximate number of neurons contained within the enteric nervous system compared to the spinal cord.
back:
• Approximately 100 million neurons
• Exceeds the number of neurons in the entire spinal cord
• Essential for independent GI movement and secretion control.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: The outer plexus of the enteric nervous system located specifically between the longitudinal and circular smooth muscle layers is the [___] plexus.
back: Myenteric (Auerbach's) Plexus. • Extends the entire length of the GI tract. • Primary regulator of gastrointestinal motility and muscle activity.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: A neonate fails to pass meconium and shows massive colonic distention. Histology reveals a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon. Which specific neural network is primarily missing?
back: Myenteric (Auerbach's) Plexus. • Its absence prevents the 'law of the gut' (peristalsis). • Results in Hirschsprung's disease (megacolon).

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Explain how the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus regulates the internal environment of a specific gut segment.
back: • Integrates sensory signals from the epithelium. • Controls local intestinal secretion and absorption. • Regulates local blood flow and mucosal infolding via submucosal muscle contraction.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: In the context of the 'law of the gut', contrast the physiological role of the myenteric plexus with the submucosal plexus.
back: • Myenteric: Coordinates long-distance propulsive peristaltic waves and tonic gut wall contractions. • Submucosal: Manages minute segmental functions like local secretion and mucosal surface changes.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Identify the specific inhibitory neurotransmitter released by myenteric neurons to relax gastrointestinal sphincters.
back: Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) or Nitric Oxide. • These signals inhibit sphincters like the pyloric and ileocecal valves to allow food progression.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: The inner plexus of the enteric nervous system, primarily concerned with controlling secretion and local blood flow, is the [___] plexus.
back: Meissner's (Submucosal) Plexus. • Located in the submucosa layer. • Acts as the primary integrator for epithelial sensory signals.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: A patient presents with dysphagia; diagnostic studies show a failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax due to localized neural damage. Identify the plexus involved.
back: Myenteric (Auerbach's) Plexus. • Loss of inhibitory neurons here prevents 'receptive relaxation'. • Diagnosed as Achalasia.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: Describe the mechanism by which the myenteric plexus increases the 'velocity of conduction' of excitatory waves.
back: • Stimulation increases the rate of rhythmic contractions. • Enhances the speed of peristaltic wave propagation. • Coordinates electrical signals across the muscular syncytium.

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Enteric Nervous System
front: Distinguish between the anatomical layers housing the myenteric plexus versus the Meissner's plexus.
back: • Myenteric: Muscularis externa (between longitudinal and circular muscle layers). • Meissner's: Submucosa layer (located between the circular muscle and mucosa).

category: Differentiate between myenteric and Meissner’s plexuses
front: List two primary physiological effects observed when the myenteric plexus is stimulated to increase motility.
back: • Increased tonic contraction (tone) of the gut wall. • Increased intensity and frequency of rhythmic contractions.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: The [___] plexus, also known as Auerbach’s plexus, is situated between the longitudinal and circular smooth muscle layers of the gastrointestinal wall.
back:
Myenteric plexus.

* Extends the entire length of the gut.
* Primarily controls gastrointestinal motility.
* Regulates muscle activity along the gut length.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: A 45-year-old male presents with difficulty swallowing and a megaesophagus. This condition typically results from damage to the neural network of the [___] plexus.
back:
Myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus.

* Specifically seen in Achalasia.
* Damage prevents "receptive relaxation" of the gastroesophageal sphincter.
* Leads to spastic contraction and functional obstruction.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: Describe the primary motor effects observed when the myenteric plexus is stimulated along the gastrointestinal tract.
back:
* Increased tonic contraction (tone) of the gut wall.
* Increased intensity and rate of rhythmic contractions.
* Increased velocity of conduction of excitatory waves (faster peristalsis).

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: Distinguish between the myenteric and submucosal plexuses based on their primary physiological roles in gastrointestinal control.
back:
* Myenteric (Auerbach’s): Controls gastrointestinal motility and muscle activity along the gut.
* Submucosal (Meissner’s): Controls local secretion, absorption, and local blood flow within each segment.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: Name the primary excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters secreted by enteric neurons in the gut wall.
back:
* Excitatory: Acetylcholine (ACh).
* Inhibitory: Norepinephrine (NE).
* Other Inhibitors: Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) and Nitric Oxide (NO).

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: The [___] plexus is located specifically within the submucosa and is primarily concerned with controlling local intestinal secretion and submucosal muscle contraction.
back:
Submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus.

* Integrated with sensory signals from gut epithelium.
* Regulates mucosal infolding.
* Controls local intestinal blood flow.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: A newborn fails to pass meconium and exhibits a massively distended colon. Biopsy reveals a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal sigmoid colon. Identify the condition.
back:
Hirschsprung’s Disease (Megacolon).

* Caused by lack of myenteric/submucosal plexuses.
* Results in failure of defecation reflexes.
* Causes upstream fecal accumulation and distention.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: Explain how the sympathetic nervous system exerts its major inhibitory effect on gastrointestinal motor function.
back:
* Secretes Norepinephrine.
* Exerts a minor direct inhibitory effect on smooth muscle.
* Exerts a major inhibitory effect on the neurons of the entire Enteric Nervous System.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: Contrast the distribution of the cranial and sacral divisions of the parasympathetic supply to the Enteric Nervous System.
back:
* Cranial (Vagus): Innervates esophagus, stomach, pancreas, and first half of the large intestine.
* Sacral (Pelvic): Innervates distal large intestine, rectum, and anus; mediates defecation reflexes.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
front: Explain why the enteric nervous system is described as possessing independent functional capabilities.
back:
* Contains >100 million neurons.
* Can control gut movement/secretion even after extrinsic nerves are severed.
* Integrates local sensory reflexes entirely within the gut wall.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
coreConcept: Interstitial Cells of Cajal as GI pacemakers
front: The specialized pacemaker cells responsible for generating the basic electrical rhythm (slow waves) in the gastrointestinal tract are the [___].
back:
Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICC).
- Form a branching network between muscle layers.
- Undergo cyclic membrane potential changes via unique pacemaker ion channels.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: A researcher observes rhythmic electrical oscillations at a frequency of 12 per minute in a segment of the human small intestine. This recording is most likely taken from the [___].
back:
Duodenum.
- Slow wave frequency varies by region:
- Stomach: 3/min
- Duodenum: 12/min
- Terminal Ileum: 8–9/min

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Explain the physiological process within Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICC) that initiates a slow wave.
back:
Unique ion channels in ICC periodically open to produce inward pacemaker currents.
- This causes cyclic, undulating changes in the resting membrane potential (5–15 mV intensity).

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Contrast 'Slow Waves' with 'Spike Potentials' regarding their ability to induce mechanical muscle contraction.
back:
Slow waves: Usually do not cause contraction (except in stomach); they dictate rhythm.
- Spike potentials: True action potentials involving Calcium entry that directly trigger muscle contraction.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Name three physiological factors that cause depolarization (increased excitability) of the gastrointestinal smooth muscle membrane.
back:
1. Muscle stretch (distention).
2. Acetylcholine (parasympathetic stimulation).
3. Specific GI hormones (e.g., Gastrin).

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Gastrointestinal spike potentials occur automatically when the resting membrane potential becomes more positive than approximately [___] millivolts.
back:
-40 mV.
- Normal resting potential: -50 to -60 mV.
- Slow waves must reach this threshold to trigger spikes.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: A patient in hemorrhagic shock exhibits severely decreased GI motility. Identify the primary neurotransmitter and its effect on the smooth muscle membrane potential.
back:
Norepinephrine (Sympathetic stimulation).
- Causes hyperpolarization of the membrane.
- Makes the muscle less excitable, inhibiting motility and movement.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Describe how the intensity of a slow wave peak influences the frequency of the resulting spike potentials.
back:
The higher the slow wave potential rises above -40 mV, the greater the frequency of spikes.
- Frequency typically ranges between 1 and 10 spikes per second.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Contrast the ion channels responsible for GI spike potentials versus those in skeletal nerve fibers.
back:
GI spikes: Calcium-sodium channels (slow to open/close; long duration).
- Nerve fibers: Fast sodium channels (rapid entry; short duration).

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: State the typical frequency of slow waves in the body of the stomach.
back:
3 per minute.
- This frequency determines the basic rhythm of gastric mixing and emptying contractions.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: The enteric nervous system plexus primarily responsible for controlling gastrointestinal secretion and local blood flow is the [___] plexus.
back:
Meissner’s plexus (or submucosal plexus).
- Located in the submucosa layer.
- Controls local absorption and glandular secretion.
- Regulates local blood flow and mucosal folding.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: A newborn presents with failure to pass meconium and colonic dilation. Histology shows an absence of ganglion cells in the submucosa. Identify the affected plexus and its primary physiological role.
back:
Meissner’s (submucosal) plexus.
- Primarily controls inner wall functions.
- Integrates sensory signals from the epithelium.
- Regulates secretion and local submucosal muscle contraction.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Explain how Meissner’s plexus regulates the rate of intestinal secretion in response to luminal contents.
back:
- Sensory neurons detect tactile or chemical stimuli.
- Signals are integrated within the submucosal plexus.
- Secretomotor neurons stimulate glands and increase local blood flow.
- Facilitates nutrient transport and mucosal protection.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Contrast the functional outcomes of a lesion in the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus versus a lesion restricted to Meissner’s plexus.
back:
- Myenteric: Impairs motility, tone, and peristaltic velocity.
- Meissner’s: Impairs local secretion, absorption, and mucosal blood flow.
- Contrast: Myenteric = GI Motility; Meissner's = Secretion/Absorption.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Specify the effect of strong sympathetic stimulation on the secretory activity mediated by Meissner's plexus.
back:
- Inhibits secretion.
- Norepinephrine directly inhibits enteric neurons.
- Indirectly reduces secretion through powerful vasoconstriction.
- Can block movement of food through inhibitory effects.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
coreConcept: Histological layers of the GI wall
front: Meissner’s plexus is primarily located within the [___] layer of the gastrointestinal wall.
back:
Submucosa.
- Positioned between the circular muscle and the mucosa.
- Contains sensory nerve endings originating in the epithelium.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: A patient experiences profuse watery diarrhea after ingesting a chemical irritant. Which plexus is responsible for detecting the irritant and coordinating the rapid electrolyte/fluid response?
back:
Meissner’s (submucosal) plexus.
- Epithelial sensory fibers detect irritation.
- Local reflexes increase intestinal secretion.
- Rapidly dilutes and washes away irritant substances.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: How does Meissner’s plexus contribute to increasing the mucosal surface area for absorption?
back:
- Controls the muscularis mucosae.
- Causes localized contractions (infolding).
- Increases epithelial surface area exposed to chyme.
- Enhances nutrient absorption efficiency.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Contrast Meissner’s plexus and the Myenteric plexus regarding their anatomical arrangement throughout the GI tract.
back:
- Myenteric: Linear chain of interconnecting neurons extending the full length.
- Meissner's: Localized segments focused on minute inner-wall function.
- Both receive extrinsic autonomic inputs.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Specify the primary neurotransmitter released by parasympathetic preganglionic fibers that excites Meissner’s plexus neurons.
back:
Acetylcholine.
- Increases activity of the entire ENS.
- Enhances rate of secretion.
- Generally promotes gastrointestinal digestive functions.

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: The Meissner’s plexus is an inner network of enteric neurons primarily located within the [___] layer of the gastrointestinal wall.
back:
- Submucosa
- Controls local secretion and absorption
- Regulates local mucosal blood flow and mucosal folding

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: A neonate fails to pass meconium, and a biopsy shows a congenital absence of enteric neurons in the submucosa. This finding primarily indicates a defect in the [___] plexus.
back:
- Meissner’s (Submucosal) plexus
- Results in impaired local secretion and mucosal blood flow
- Characteristic of Hirschsprung’s disease

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Explain the primary physiological mechanism by which the Meissner’s plexus regulates the intestinal luminal environment.
back:
- Integrates sensory signals from the epithelium
- Stimulates local glandular secretion
- Controls local absorption and infolding of the mucosa

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Contrast the primary functional focus of the Meissner’s plexus with that of the Myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus.
back:
- Meissner’s: Local secretion, absorption, and mucosal blood flow
- Myenteric: GIT motility (tone, intensity, and rate of contractions)

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Predict the effect of parasympathetic vagal stimulation on the glandular output controlled by the Meissner’s plexus.
back:
- Increases secretory rate
- Enhances enteric neuronal activity
- Mediated primarily by acetylcholine (ACh)

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Sensory signals originating from the gastrointestinal epithelium or gut wall are integrated within the [___] plexus to control minute segments of the intestine.
back:
- Submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus
- Triggers local mucosal muscle contraction
- Facilitates site-specific absorption

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: A patient in a sympathetic 'fight or flight' state experiences a significant decrease in intestinal secretions. This occurs because norepinephrine primarily [___] the Meissner's plexus.
back:
- Inhibits the neurons
- Directly constricts mucosal blood vessels
- Suppresses overall secretory activity

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Describe the specific role of the Meissner’s plexus in local reflexes initiated by chemical irritation of the gut mucosa.
back:
- Receives afferent signals from epithelial receptors
- Triggers compensatory glandular secretion
- Stimulates local vasodilation to dilute irritants

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Distinguish the anatomical boundaries of the Meissner’s plexus from the Myenteric plexus relative to the intestinal muscle layers.
back:
- Meissner’s: Inner plexus located in the submucosa
- Myenteric: Outer plexus between longitudinal and circular muscle layers

category: Describe the Meissner’s plexus
front: Identify the neurotransmitter released by the Meissner’s plexus that most often excites gastrointestinal secretory activity.
back:
- Acetylcholine (ACh)
- Increases enzyme and mucus release
- Opposed by inhibitory sympathetic norepinephrine

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Anatomical location and primary function of the myenteric plexus.
front: The enteric nervous system plexus primarily responsible for controlling gastrointestinal movements and located between the longitudinal and circular smooth muscle layers is the [___] plexus.
back:
Myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus).
- Extends the entire length of the GI tract.
- Controls muscle activity (tone, intensity, and rate of contractions).
- Increases velocity of conduction of excitatory waves.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Clinical correlation of ENS deficiency in Hirschsprung's disease.
front: A newborn presents with failure to pass meconium and abdominal distension. Biopsy reveals a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon. This condition, Hirschsprung’s disease, primarily involves a defect in the [___].
back:
Enteric Nervous System (Myenteric and Submucosal plexuses).
- Results from failure of neural crest cell migration.
- Leads to lack of peristalsis in affected segments.
- Causes functional obstruction and megacolon.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Functional role of the submucosal plexus in GI secretion and blood flow.
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus regulates the internal environment of a specific gut segment.
back:
- Integrates sensory signals from the gastrointestinal epithelium.
- Controls local intestinal secretion and absorption.
- Regulates local blood flow.
- Controls local contraction of the submucosal muscle for mucosal infolding.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Differential functions of the two major enteric plexuses.
front: Distinguish the functional effects of the myenteric plexus from the submucosal plexus during the digestive process.
back:
- Myenteric: Focuses on motor activity (tone and peristalsis velocity).
- Submucosal: Focuses on secretory activity and local sensory integration.
- Myenteric lies between muscle layers; Submucosal lies in the submucosa.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Sympathetic modulation of the Enteric Nervous System.
front: Describe the dual mechanism by which sympathetic stimulation inhibits gastrointestinal activity via the enteric nervous system.
back:
- Direct Effect: Secreted norepinephrine directly inhibits intestinal smooth muscle (except mucosal muscle).
- Indirect/Major Effect: Inhibitory effect of norepinephrine on neurons of the entire enteric nervous system.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Primary excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters of the ENS.
front: In the enteric nervous system, [___] is the neurotransmitter that most often excites gastrointestinal activity, while [___] almost always inhibits it.
back:
- Acetylcholine (Excitatory).
- Norepinephrine (Inhibitory).
- Norepinephrine enters the gut mainly via sympathetic nerves or the adrenal medulla.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Dependency of GI motility on cholinergic ENS pathways.
front: A patient is treated with Atropine to manage excessive secretions. Predict the effect of this drug on the 'Law of the Gut' (peristaltic reflex).
back:
- Peristaltic waves are greatly depressed or blocked.
- Atropine paralyzes cholinergic nerve endings in the myenteric plexus.
- Highlights that effectual peristalsis requires an active, functional ENS.

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Role of inhibitory ENS neurons in polarized GI motility.
front: Explain the role of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus during the 'Law of the Gut' or peristaltic reflex.
back:
- Secretes inhibitory transmitters like Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) or Nitric Oxide.
- Causes 'receptive relaxation' several centimeters downstream toward the anus.
- Facilitates easier propulsion of food by relaxing sphincters (pyloric/ileocecal).

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Classification of GI reflexes based on neural integration sites.
front: Contrast the origin and destination of intrinsic enteric reflexes with those of the gastrocolic and enterogastric reflexes.
back:
- Intrinsic: Integrated entirely within the gut wall ENS (controls local secretion/mixing).
- Gastrocolic/Enterogastric: Travel from gut to prevertebral sympathetic ganglia and back to the gut (long-distance communication).

category: Classify the components of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Sensory inputs triggering Enteric Nervous System reflexes.
front: List the three specific categories of stimuli that activate the sensory nerve endings originating in the gut wall or epithelium.
back:
- Irritation of the gut mucosa.
- Excessive distention of the gut wall.
- Presence of specific chemical substances in the gut lumen.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: The specialized pacemaker cells located between smooth muscle layers that undergo cyclic membrane potential changes to generate slow waves are the [___].
back:
• Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC).
• Form a network connected via gap junctions.
• Act as the electrical pacemakers of the gut.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: A researcher monitors duodenal electrical activity and observes rhythmic oscillations at 12 per minute that fail to trigger contractions. Identify these oscillations and their primary cause.
back:
• Slow waves.
• Caused by cyclic opening of unique ion channels producing inward pacemaker currents.
• These are not true action potentials.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Explain how slow waves determine the maximum frequency of gastrointestinal contractions.
back:
• They set the basic electrical rhythm (BER).
• Spike potentials (true APs) only occur at the peaks of slow waves.
• Contractions generally only follow spike potentials.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Contrast the ionic basis and physiological outcome of a slow wave peak reaching -40 mV versus remaining below this threshold.
back:
• At -40 mV: Threshold is reached; calcium-sodium channels open; spike potentials trigger contraction.
• Below -40 mV: No spike potentials occur; no contraction (except in stomach); only undulation in potential.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Describe the regional variations in slow wave frequency from the stomach to the ileum.
back:
• Stomach: ~3/min.
• Duodenum: ~12/min.
• Terminal Ileum: 8 to 9/min.
• Reflects the local rhythm of motility.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Gastrointestinal slow waves are characterized by an intensity typically ranging between [___] millivolts.
back:
• 5 to 15 millivolts.
• Resting membrane potential is usually -50 to -60 mV.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: A biopsy reveals a deficiency in the myenteric plexus and Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICC). Predict the most likely alteration in gut electrical dynamics.
back:
• Absence of slow wave generation.
• Loss of rhythmic coordination of contractions.
• Impaired spike potential initiation.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Explain the role of the electrical syncytium in the propagation of slow waves across the circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
back:
• Gap junctions allow low-resistance ion movement.
• Excitation in one layer often excites the other.
• Allows electrical signals to travel centimeters to meters along the gut.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: Distinguish between the ionic currents responsible for the slow wave itself versus the spike potentials that appear on its peaks.
back:
• Slow Waves: Primarily involve cyclic sodium-dominant pacemaker currents.
• Spike Potentials: Caused by slow calcium-sodium channels; involve significant calcium entry.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing slow wave
front: State the standard resting membrane potential range for gastrointestinal smooth muscle fibers.
back:
• -50 to -60 millivolts.
• Average is typically cited as -56 mV.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
coreConcept: Inhibitory Neurotransmitters of the Myenteric Plexus
front: The primary inhibitory neurotransmitter released by myenteric neurons to facilitate the relaxation of intestinal sphincters is [___].
back:
• Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP).
• Nitric Oxide (NO).
• These allow food to pass between successive segments of the GI tract.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: A 45-year-old male presents with persistent dysphagia and a 'bird’s beak' appearance on barium swallow. Destruction of the myenteric plexus in the lower esophagus is suspected. Identify the condition.
back:
• Achalasia cardia.
• Pathophysiology: Loss of myenteric neurons results in failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Describe the primary motor effects observed in the gastrointestinal wall when the myenteric plexus is stimulated.
back:
• Increased tonic contraction (tone).
• Increased intensity and rate of rhythmic contractions.
• Increased velocity of conduction of excitatory waves (peristalsis).

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: A laboratory model involves the selective destruction of Auerbach’s plexus while leaving Meissner’s plexus intact. Contrast the expected functional deficits.
back:
• Auerbach (Myenteric): Loss of gut motility and peristaltic waves.
• Meissner (Submucosal): GI secretion and local blood flow control remain largely preserved.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Identify the pharmacological consequence of administering Atropine on myenteric plexus-mediated peristalsis.
back:
• Blocks cholinergic (Acetylcholine) nerve endings.
• Result: Effectively paralyzes or greatly depresses propulsive movements (peristalsis) throughout the gut.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: The congenital absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of the distal colon leads to the diagnostic presentation of [___].
back:
• Hirschsprung's Disease (Megacolon).
• Characterized by a lack of peristaltic reflex and massive dilation of the proximal colon.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
coreConcept: Myenteric Plexus and the Law of the Gut
front: A neonate fails to pass meconium. Biopsy shows a segment of colon lacking the myenteric plexus. Predict the effect on the 'Law of the Gut' in this segment.
back:
• Absence of the 'peristaltic reflex.'
• The segment cannot initiate orad contraction or downstream receptive relaxation.
• Causes functional intestinal obstruction.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Explain how the 'Polarization' of the myenteric plexus ensures unidirectional movement of food.
back:
• Directional transmission: The plexus is polarized toward the anus.
• Downstream receptive relaxation: Allows food to move easier distally than orally.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Contrast the reflex loop of the gastrocolic reflex with the local myenteric (peristaltic) reflex.
back:
• Myenteric Reflex: Integrated entirely within the gut wall enteric nervous system.
• Gastrocolic Reflex: Signals travel from stomach to prevertebral ganglia and back to the colon.

category: Discuss the location and significance of myenteric plexus
front: Specify the exact histological location of the myenteric plexus within the gastrointestinal wall.
back:
• Situated between the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer and the inner circular smooth muscle layer.
• It extends from the esophagus to the anus.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Gastrointestinal spike potentials are true action potentials that occur automatically when the resting membrane potential becomes more positive than [___] millivolts.
back:
- -40 millivolts.
- Normal RMP is between -50 and -60 mV.
- These spikes are triggered at the peaks of slow waves.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
coreConcept: Ionic Basis of GI Spike Potentials
front: A research study observes that gastrointestinal smooth muscle action potentials last significantly longer than those in neurons. This prolonged duration is primarily due to [___].
back:
- Slow opening and closing of calcium-sodium channels.
- These channels allow large amounts of calcium to enter the cell.
- Spikes last 10-20 milliseconds (10-40x longer than nerve APs).

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Explain the role of the slow wave peak height in determining the frequency of spike potentials.
back:
- The higher the slow wave rises above the -40 mV threshold, the higher the spike frequency.
- Frequency range: 1 to 10 spikes per second.
- Spike potentials, not slow waves, trigger actual contraction.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Contrast the ionic channels responsible for depolarization in nerve fibers versus gastrointestinal smooth muscle spikes.
back:
- Nerve Fibers: Rapid entry of sodium through voltage-gated sodium channels.
- GI Smooth Muscle: Slower entry of calcium and sodium via calcium-sodium channels.
- Calcium entry is critical for GI contraction mechanism.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Describe the physiological effect of acetylcholine (ACh) on the resting membrane potential and spike potential generation.
back:
- ACh causes depolarization (makes RMP less negative).
- Moves RMP toward the -40 mV threshold.
- Increases the frequency of spike potentials and subsequent gut motility.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Hyperpolarization of the gastrointestinal smooth muscle membrane, which inhibits spike potentials, is primarily caused by [___].
back:
- Norepinephrine or Epinephrine.
- Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system.
- Moves RMP away from the threshold, making the muscle less excitable.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: A patient experiences significant intestinal distention due to a bolus. Explain how this mechanical factor influences spike potential development.
back:
- Stretching the muscle causes depolarization.
- This makes the membrane more excitable.
- Increases spike potential frequency, initiating peristaltic contractions behind the bolus.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
coreConcept: Excitation-Contraction Coupling in GI Smooth Muscle
front: Explain the precise mechanism by which a spike potential leads to a physical contraction of the smooth muscle fiber.
back:
- Entry of calcium ions during the spike potential.
- Calcium binds to calmodulin.
- This complex activates myosin filaments, creating attractive forces with actin to cause contraction.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
coreConcept: Functional Significance of GI Electrical Waves
front: Distinguish between the contractive consequences of a 'Slow Wave' peak versus a 'Spike Potential'.
back:
- Slow Waves: Usually do not cause contraction (only sodium entry).
- Spike Potentials: Cause significant calcium entry, directly exciting muscle contraction.
- Exceptions: Slow waves may cause some contraction in the stomach.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Identify the specialized cells responsible for the cyclic changes in membrane potential that allow slow waves to reach the spike potential threshold.
back:
- Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC).
- Act as electrical pacemakers for smooth muscle cells.
- They have unique ion channels that periodically produce pacemaker currents.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: The gastrointestinal smooth muscle membrane becomes more excitable and undergoes depolarization primarily under the influence of the neurotransmitter [___].
back:
* Acetylcholine
* Released from parasympathetic nerve endings
* Makes the resting membrane potential less negative
* Increases frequency of spike potentials

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: A patient in hemorrhagic shock presents with an adynamic ileus. This suppression of gut motility is caused by the hyperpolarizing effect of which catecholamines?
back:
* Norepinephrine and Epinephrine
* Secreted by sympathetic nerves and adrenal medullae
* Makes the membrane potential more negative
* Inhibits spike potential generation

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which mechanical distention of the intestinal wall initiates a contraction.
back:
* Stretching of the muscle directly depolarizes the membrane
* The resting potential becomes less negative (approaches -40 mV)
* This triggers spike potentials (action potentials)
* Leads to calcium entry and calmodulin activation

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Contrast the factors that shift the GIT resting membrane potential toward -40 mV with those that shift it toward -70 mV.
back:
* Depolarizing Factors (-40 mV): Muscle stretch, Acetylcholine, and GI hormones (Gastrin, CCK)
* Hyperpolarizing Factors (-70 mV): Norepinephrine, Epinephrine, and Sympathetic stimulation

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Identify the specific gastrointestinal hormones known to serve as depolarizing factors to increase gut excitability.
back:
* Gastrin
* Cholecystokinin (CCK)
* Motilin
* These increase excitability by making the RMP less negative

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: The baseline resting membrane potential of the gut smooth muscle, normally averaging [___] mV, must be reduced to reach the threshold for spike potentials.
back:
* -56 millivolts
* Normal range is -50 to -60 mV
* Threshold for spikes is approximately -40 mV
* Depolarization brings the RMP closer to threshold

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
coreConcept: Cholinergic influence on GIT electrical activity
front: A research animal is administered a drug that blocks nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. Describe the expected change in the smooth muscle's electrical baseline.
back:
* Loss of the depolarizing effect of Acetylcholine
* The membrane becomes more negative/less excitable
* Reduction in spike potential frequency
* Decreased tonic and rhythmic contractions

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
coreConcept: Ionic basis of GIT electrical waves
front: How does the ionic basis of depolarization during a 'slow wave' differ from the depolarization during a 'spike potential'?
back:
* Slow Waves: Caused by cyclic sodium entry via Interstitial Cells of Cajal
* Spike Potentials: Caused by large entry of Calcium via calcium-sodium channels
* Spikes occur only when slow wave peaks exceed -40 mV

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Distinguish between the effects of the Vagus nerve and the Celiac ganglion on the excitability of the gastric membrane.
back:
* Vagus Nerve: Parasympathetic; releases Acetylcholine; causes depolarization
* Celiac Ganglion: Sympathetic; releases Norepinephrine; causes hyperpolarization

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Summarize the two primary ways the sympathetic nervous system achieves hyperpolarization of the gut wall.
back:
* Direct effect of norepinephrine on smooth muscle fibers
* Indirect inhibitory effect on the neurons of the enteric nervous system
* Both increase the negativity of the membrane potential

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: In the gastrointestinal tract, the resting membrane potential becomes less negative (depolarizes) and more excitable when the smooth muscle undergoes [___].
back:
* Stretching (distention).
* Results in increased spike potential frequency.
* Enhances muscular contractions.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: A patient in a high-stress 'fight-or-flight' state experiences reduced gut motility. Explain the underlying change in the smooth muscle membrane potential.
back:
* Hyperpolarization.
* Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine.
* Membrane becomes more negative and less excitable.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Explain how Acetylcholine (ACh) released from parasympathetic nerve endings increases the motor activity of the gut wall.
back:
* Stimulates depolarization of the membrane.
* Shifts resting membrane potential (RMP) toward -40 mV.
* Increases frequency of action potentials (spikes).

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Contrast the effect of intestinal distention versus sympathetic trunk stimulation on the baseline voltage of the myenteric syncytium.
back:
* Distention: Causes depolarization (baseline shifts upward).
* Sympathetic Stimulation: Causes hyperpolarization (baseline shifts downward).
* Distention excites motility; sympathetics inhibit it.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Name the two primary catecholamines that cause the gastrointestinal membrane potential to become more negative.
back:
* Norepinephrine.
* Epinephrine.
* Both lead to hyperpolarization and reduced muscle excitability.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: The GIT smooth muscle membrane is considered hyperpolarized when its resting potential moves from -56 mV to a value such as [___].
back:
* A more negative value (e.g., -65 mV or -70 mV).
* This makes the muscle fiber less excitable.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: During surgery, manual irritation of the peritoneum causes general inhibition of gut movements. This is achieved by shifting the membrane potential towards [___].
back:
* Hyperpolarization.
* Mediated by sympathetic reflexes.
* Decreases probability of reaching threshold for spike potentials.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Describe the relationship between hormonal stimulation and the generation of tonic contractions in certain gut segments.
back:
* Hormones cause continuous partial depolarization.
* This can occur without generating full action potentials.
* Results in sustained, long-term muscle contraction.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: Contrast the functional outcome of membrane depolarization at -40 mV versus the normal resting potential of -56 mV.
back:
* At -40 mV: Threshold is reached; spike potentials occur.
* At -56 mV: Baseline resting state; no action potentials generated.
* Depolarization is the bridge between rest and contraction.

category: Enlist the factors that depolarize & hyperpolarize the GIT membrane
front: List three specific factors that make the gastrointestinal smooth muscle membrane more excitable.
back:
1. Muscle stretch (distention).
2. Acetylcholine release.
3. Specific GI hormones (e.g., Gastrin).

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Parasympathetic nerves typically increase gastrointestinal activity by releasing the neurotransmitter [___] from their endings.
back:
• Acetylcholine (ACh)
• It primarily excites gastrointestinal activity by stimulating the enteric nervous system.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: A patient in circulatory shock shows significantly reduced gastrointestinal motility and secretion. This is primarily mediated by the sympathetic release of [___] which inhibits the enteric nervous system.
back:
• Norepinephrine
• It acts both directly on smooth muscle and indirectly by inhibiting enteric neurons.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Describe the two ways sympathetic stimulation inhibits gastrointestinal activity.
back:
• Direct effect: Secreted norepinephrine inhibits intestinal smooth muscle (except mucosal muscle).
• Major effect: Norepinephrine inhibits neurons of the entire enteric nervous system.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Contrast the anatomical distribution of the cranial parasympathetic system versus the sacral parasympathetic system in the gut.
back:
• Cranial (Vagus): Esophagus, stomach, pancreas, and proximal half of the large intestine.
• Sacral (S2-S4/Pelvic nerves): Distal half of the large intestine to the anus.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Explain why atropine treatment results in the failure of effectual peristalsis.
back:
• It blocks cholinergic (ACh) receptors.
• This paralyzes the excitatory cholinergic nerve endings of the myenteric plexus required for the peristaltic reflex.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: In the gastrointestinal tract, the postganglionic neurons of the parasympathetic system are located within the [___].
back: • Enteric Nervous System (specifically the Myenteric and Submucosal plexuses).

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
coreConcept: Sympathetic Control of Splanchnic Blood Flow
front: A patient undergoing an abdominal procedure experiences intense sympathetic stimulation. Predict the effect on gastrointestinal blood flow and why this occurs.
back:
• Intense vasoconstriction of arterioles occurs.
• This significantly decreases local blood flow to divert volume to skeletal muscle or heart.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Explain the role of vagal afferent fibers in controlling gastrointestinal function.
back:
• 80% of vagal fibers are afferent.
• They transmit sensory signals (irritation, distention) to the medulla to initiate vagal reflex responses.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Distinguish the effect of sympathetic stimulation on the main intestinal smooth muscle layers versus the mucosal muscle.
back:
• Main smooth muscle layers: Inhibited/relaxed.
• Mucosal muscle: Stimulated/excited.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Name the spinal cord segments that provide the sympathetic fibers to the gastrointestinal tract.
back:
• T5 to L2
• Fibers pass through sympathetic chains to prevertebral ganglia (Celiac/Mesenteric).

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Gastrointestinal spike potentials are initiated automatically when the resting membrane potential becomes more positive than [___] millivolts.
back:
• -40 millivolts.
• Normal resting potential is -50 to -60 mV.
• Values less negative than -40 mV trigger these true action potentials.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: A patient exhibits increased intestinal motility after parasympathetic stimulation. Describe the electrical transition from slow waves to contraction in this scenario.
back:
• Acetylcholine depolarizes the membrane.
• When slow wave peaks exceed -40 mV, spike potentials fire.
• These spikes allow calcium entry via slow channels, triggering mechanical contraction.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Explain the role of calcium-sodium channels in the generation and duration of GIT spike potentials.
back:
• They allow large amounts of Calcium and small amounts of Sodium to enter.
• These channels open and close much slower than nerve sodium channels.
• This slowness causes the long duration (10–20 milliseconds) of spikes.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Contrast the action potentials of large nerve fibers with GIT spike potentials regarding duration and ion channel types.
back:
• Nerve: Very short (~1 ms); rapid voltage-gated Sodium channels.
• GIT Spikes: Long (10–20 ms); slow Calcium-Sodium channels.
• GIT spikes last 10–40 times longer than nerve action potentials.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
coreConcept: Slow Wave and Spike Frequency Relationship
front: How does the height of a slow wave affect the frequency of spike potential discharge?
back:
• Higher slow wave peaks (above -40 mV) lead to higher spike frequencies.
• Frequency ranges from 1 to 10 spikes per second.
• Spikes only appear at the undulating peaks of slow waves.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Gastrointestinal smooth muscle contraction is primarily dependent on the influx of [___] ions during the spike potential.
back:
• Calcium ions (Ca2+).
• Unlike slow waves (sodium only), spikes facilitate significant calcium entry.
• Calcium activates the calmodulin-myosin mechanism for contraction.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: A research study finds that sympathetic stimulation causes gut stasis. Apply your knowledge of membrane potentials to explain this inhibitory mechanism.
back:
• Norepinephrine/Epinephrine cause membrane hyperpolarization.
• The resting potential becomes more negative (further from -40 mV).
• This prevents slow waves from reaching the threshold required to fire spike potentials.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Explain the mechanism by which physical stretching of the intestinal wall leads to the development of spike potentials.
back:
• Stretch directly depolarizes the smooth muscle membrane.
• This shifts the resting potential closer to the -40 mV threshold.
• Spike potential frequency increases, resulting in localized propulsive contractions.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Distinguish between 'slow waves' and 'spike potentials' in terms of their ability to generate gastrointestinal motility.
back:
• Slow Waves: Not action potentials; do not cause contraction (except in stomach).
• Spike Potentials: True action potentials; cause muscle contraction via calcium influx.

category: Explain the mechanism of developing spike potential
front: Identify the specific intracellular protein that acts as the calcium sensor to initiate contraction following a spike potential.
back:
• Calmodulin.
• Entering Calcium binds to Calmodulin.
• This complex activates myosin filaments, developing the attractive forces required for muscle contraction.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: The primary neurotransmitter released by enteric neurons to stimulate gastrointestinal motility and secretion is [___].
back:
Acetylcholine (ACh).
- Principal excitatory neurotransmitter.
- Increases gut wall tone and contraction frequency.
- Stimulates glandular secretion.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: A 30-year-old male with persistent GERD undergoes manometry showing failed relaxation of the Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES). A deficiency in which inhibitory enteric transmitter is likely?
back:
Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) or Nitric Oxide (NO).
- Major inhibitory transmitters in ENS.
- Mediate receptive relaxation.
- Allow sphincters to open for bolus passage.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which Norepinephrine (NE) inhibits gastrointestinal activity.
back:
1. Direct Effect: Mildly inhibits intestinal smooth muscle (except mucosal muscle).
2. Major Effect: Potent inhibition of enteric neurons.
- Blocks the entire Enteric Nervous System (ENS) signaling cascade.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Contrast the primary physiological roles of the Myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus with the Submucosal (Meissner's) plexus regarding neurotransmitter-mediated effects.
back:
Myenteric: Primarily controls gastrointestinal motility, muscle tone, and contraction velocity.
Submucosal: Primarily regulates local intestinal secretion, absorption, and local blood flow.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Enlist the excitatory neuropeptide that often works alongside Acetylcholine to increase gut motility.
back:
Substance P.
- Potent excitatory transmitter.
- Enhances smooth muscle contraction.
- Found in sensory and motor enteric neurons.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Gaseous inhibitory signaling in the enteric nervous system is primarily mediated by [___].
back:
Nitric Oxide (NO).
- Non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic (NANC) inhibitor.
- Essential for sphincter relaxation.
- Synthesized on demand by enteric neurons.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: A neonate presents with failure to pass meconium and a narrowed segment of distal colon. The histological absence of what structures explains the lack of peristalsis?
back:
Enteric Neurons (Myenteric and Submucosal plexuses).
- Diagnosis: Hirschsprung’s Disease.
- Leads to failure of VIP/NO-mediated relaxation.
- Causes functional obstruction.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: How do enkephalins (Leu-enkephalin and Met-enkephalin) influence the movement of food through the alimentary tract?
back:
Inhibitory neurotransmitters.
- They generally slow intestinal transit.
- Often targeted by anti-diarrheal medications.
- Regulate the release of other transmitters.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Distinguish the effect of Norepinephrine on the gastrointestinal 'mucosal muscle' compared to the 'longitudinal/circular muscle' layers.
back:
Mucosal Muscle: Norepinephrine is EXCITATORY (causes contraction).
Longitudinal/Circular Muscle: Norepinephrine is INHIBITORY (causes relaxation).

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Name the three key stimuli detected by ENS sensory neurons that trigger local enteric reflexes.
back:
1. Distention (Stretch) of the gut wall.
2. Irritation of the gut mucosa.
3. Presence of specific chemical substances in the lumen.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Parasympathetic stimulation typically excites gastrointestinal activity through the release of the neurotransmitter [___].
back:
Acetylcholine (ACh).
- Primary excitatory neurotransmitter.
- Increases motility and enhances glandular secretion rates.
- Acts via postganglionic neurons in the enteric plexuses.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: A 45-year-old male presents with dysphagia and a 'bird's beak' appearance on barium swallow. Pathophysiological damage to which specific neural structure causes the failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax?
back:
Myenteric (Auerbach's) Plexus.
- Loss of inhibitory neurons.
- Deficiency in VIP or Nitric Oxide release.
- Leads to chronic tonic contraction (Achalasia).

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which sympathetic stimulation inhibits gastrointestinal function.
back:
1. Direct effect: Norepinephrine inhibits smooth muscle (except mucosal muscle).
2. Major effect: Inhibits neurons of the entire enteric nervous system.
- Result: Decreased motility and reduced secretions.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Contrast the anatomical distribution and primary roles of Cranial versus Sacral parasympathetic fibers in the gut.
back:
Cranial (Vagus): Supplies esophagus to proximal half of large intestine; enhances general motility/secretion.
Sacral (Pelvic): Supplies distal large intestine to anus; primarily executes defecation reflexes.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Explain why intense sympathetic stimulation only temporarily reduces gastrointestinal blood flow despite continuous vasoconstrictor signals.
back:
Autoregulatory Escape.
- Local metabolic vasodilators (e.g., adenosine) accumulate during ischemia.
- These factors override sympathetic vasoconstriction.
- Restores nutrient blood flow to glands and muscle.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Sympathetic fibers providing inhibitory control to the gastrointestinal tract originate in the spinal cord between segments [___].
back:
T5 and L2.
- Preganglionic fibers pass through sympathetic chains.
- Postganglionic cell bodies reside in celiac and mesenteric ganglia.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: A student experiencing severe 'examination nerves' develops frequent, watery diarrhea. This condition is primarily mediated by which autonomic pathway?
back:
Parasympathetic overstimulation (Psychogenic Diarrhea).
- Greatly excites motility in the distal colon.
- Stimulates excess mucus secretion.
- Result of emotional stress on the medullary centers.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: How do vagal afferent fibers facilitate the 'pyloric pump' and gastric emptying in response to stomach distention?
back:
Vagovagal Reflex.
- 80% of vagal fibers are afferent (sensory).
- Distention signals reach the brainstem.
- Efferent signals return to increase antral contractions and relax the pylorus.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: Contrast the primary functions of the Myenteric (Auerbach's) and Submucosal (Meissner's) plexuses.
back:
Myenteric: Located between muscle layers; controls GIT motility (tone and contraction intensity).
Submucosal: Located in submucosa; controls local secretion, absorption, and mucosal blood flow.

category: Explain the role of sympathetic & parasympathetic nervous system in controlling GIT function
front: State the effect of sympathetic stimulation on the 'muscularis mucosae' compared to the rest of the GIT smooth muscle.
back:
It excites the mucosal muscle.
- This is an exception to the general sympathetic inhibitory rule.
- Assists in local mucosal folding and villar 'milking'.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: The [___] reflex is a long-distance reflex initiated by stomach distention that signals the colon to evacuate its contents, typically following a meal.
back:
• Gastrocolic reflex
• Mediated via the autonomic nervous system
• Stimulates mass movements in the colon
• Facilitates the urge to defecate after eating.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: A patient with acute appendicitis presents with a 'silent abdomen' (absent bowel sounds). Which reflex is responsible for this generalized intestinal inhibition?
back:
• Peritoneointestinal reflex
• Triggered by peritoneal irritation/inflammation
• Strongly inhibits excitatory enteric nerves
• Leads to functional intestinal paralysis (ileus).

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: How does the enterogastric reflex modulate gastric function when chyme with a pH of less than 3.5 enters the duodenum?
back:
• Inhibits the 'pyloric pump' (antral contractions)
• Increases pyloric sphincter tone
• Slows gastric emptying
• Protects the duodenum from excessive acidity.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Distinguish between the gastroileal and colonoileal reflexes regarding their impact on the ileocecal valve.
back:
• Gastroileal: Stomach distention intensifies ileal peristalsis to force chyme into the cecum.
• Colonoileal: Cecal distention inhibits ileal peristalsis and excites the sphincter to prevent backflow.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Detail the physiological steps of the vagovagal reflex during the storage phase of gastric motility.
back:
• Stimulated by gastric wall stretch
• Signals travel to brainstem and back via vagus
• Reduces muscular tone in the gastric body
• Allows 'receptive relaxation' to accommodate 0.8–1.5L of food.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: The intrinsic defecation reflex is mediated entirely within the [___], while the more powerful parasympathetic defecation reflex involves the sacral spinal cord.
back:
• Enteric nervous system (Myenteric plexus)
• Intrinsic reflex is relatively weak
• Parasympathetic reflex (via pelvic nerves) is required for effective evacuation.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
coreConcept: Spinal Cord Integration of GI Reflexes
front: A patient with a spinal cord injury at the T12 level can still initiate a bowel movement via digital stimulation or enema. Explain the reflex preservation.
back:
• The sacral parasympathetic defecation reflex remains intact
• Integration occurs in the conus medullaris (S2-S4)
• Only voluntary cortical control of the external sphincter is lost.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
coreConcept: Law of the Gut / Peristaltic Reflex
front: Explain the biological mechanism of the 'Law of the Gut' during a peristaltic reflex.
back:
• Triggered by local distention
• Contractile ring forms orad (mouth-ward) to the bolus
• 'Receptive relaxation' occurs several centimeters anal-ward
• Ensures unidirectional (aboral) movement.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Contrast the integration sites of enteric reflexes versus those from the gut to the prevertebral ganglia.
back:
• Enteric Reflexes: Integrated entirely within the gut wall (secretion, mixing).
• Prevertebral Ganglia Reflexes: Integrated in sympathetic ganglia outside the gut (Gastrocolic, Enterogastric, Colonoileal).

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Identify the primary stimulus and the resultant motor response of the chewing (mastication) reflex.
back:
• Stimulus: Presence of food bolus in the oral cavity
• Response: Reflex inhibition of jaw muscles (jaw drops)
• Rebound: Triggered stretch reflex causes jaw closure.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: The primary neurotransmitter released by the enteric nervous system that specifically mediates relaxation of gastrointestinal sphincters and promotes receptive relaxation is [___].
back:
* Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP).
* Nitric Oxide (NO) also acts as a key inhibitory gas.
* These facilitate food movement by opening sphincters (e.g., pylorus, ileocecal valve).

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: A neonate fails to pass meconium and shows massive colonic distention. Histology reveals an absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus. This condition results in a lack of which specific inhibitory signals required for defecation?
back:
* Diagnosis: Hirschsprung’s Disease (Megacolon).
* Lack of VIP and Nitric Oxide.
* Leads to failure of the internal anal sphincter to relax.
* Causes tonic contraction and functional obstruction.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Explain the opposing roles of Acetylcholine (ACh) and Norepinephrine (NE) in the regulation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle excitability.
back:
* ACh: Excitatory; depolarizes smooth muscle membranes to increase motility and secretion.
* NE: Inhibitory; hyperpolarizes membranes to decrease activity.
* ACh is the primary intrinsic/parasympathetic transmitter; NE is the primary sympathetic transmitter.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Contrast the effects of Substance P and Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) on the smooth muscle of the intestinal wall.
back:
* Substance P: Excitatory neurotransmitter; causes contraction of intestinal smooth muscle.
* VIP: Inhibitory neurotransmitter; causes relaxation.
* VIP is essential for 'Law of the Gut' downstream relaxation during peristalsis.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Identify the neurotransmitter being inhibited when Atropine is administered to block the contractile ring required for intestinal peristalsis.
back:
* Neurotransmitter: Acetylcholine (ACh).
* Atropine paralyzes cholinergic nerve endings in the myenteric plexus.
* This effectively blocks the peristaltic reflex and reduces gut motility.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
coreConcept: Nitric Oxide as a NANC transmitter
front: While Acetylcholine is the main excitatory transmitter, the primary non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic (NANC) inhibitory gas that facilitates smooth muscle relaxation in the ENS is [___].
back:
* Nitric Oxide (NO).
* Functions as a potent smooth muscle relaxant.
* Crucial for the relaxation phase of the peristaltic reflex and sphincter opening.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: A patient with chronic stress exhibits excessive sympathetic discharge. Describe the impact of the primary sympathetic neurotransmitter on the enteric nervous system neurons.
back:
* Increased release of Norepinephrine.
* Exerts a major inhibitory effect on ENS neurons.
* Also directly inhibits intestinal smooth muscle (except mucosal muscle).
* Results in decreased motility and possible constipation.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Detail the role of Enkephalins (Leu-enkephalin and Met-enkephalin) within the enteric nervous system regarding intestinal transit.
back:
* Generally inhibitory neuromodulators.
* Inhibit the release of excitatory transmitters like Acetylcholine.
* Result: Decreased intestinal motility and reduced fluid secretion.
* This mechanism is utilized by opioid-based anti-diarrheal medications.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Distinguish between the roles of Serotonin (5-HT) and Somatostatin within the enteric nervous system.
back:
* Serotonin (5-HT): Generally excitatory; initiates the peristaltic reflex by stimulating sensory neurons.
* Somatostatin: Primarily inhibitory; inhibits gastric acid secretion and slows overall GI motility.

category: Enlist the excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitters of enteric nervous system
front: Enlist three specific inhibitory neurotransmitters of the Enteric Nervous System (ENS) apart from Norepinephrine.
back:
* Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP).
* Nitric Oxide (NO).
* Somatostatin.
* (Also Enkephalins and Neuropeptide Y).
* These mediate smooth muscle relaxation and inhibit secretion.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: The reflex that transmits signals from the stomach to the colon to induce evacuation after a meal is the [___] reflex.
back:
• Gastrocolic reflex
• Function: Initiates mass movements in the colon after stomach distention.
• Mediated via the autonomic nervous system.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: A patient experiences delayed gastric emptying immediately after high-fat, acidic chyme enters the duodenum. Identify the primary nervous reflex and its motor outcome.
back:
• Enterogastric reflex
• Mechanism: Signals from duodenum to prevertebral ganglia and back to stomach.
• Outcome: Inhibits pyloric pump and increases pyloric sphincter tone.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Explain the biological mechanism behind the 'Law of the Gut' regarding the peristaltic reflex.
back:
• Stimulus: Local distention of the gut.
• Orad side: Contractile ring forms (myenteric reflex).
• Anal side: Receptive relaxation occurs several centimeters downstream to facilitate forward movement.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Contrast the intrinsic defecation reflex with the parasympathetic defecation reflex regarding their origin and relative potency.
back:
• Intrinsic: Mediated entirely by the local enteric nervous system; relatively weak.
• Parasympathetic: Involves sacral spinal cord (S2-S4) via pelvic nerves; highly powerful and essential for effective evacuation.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Detail the sensory triggers and motor consequences of the colonoileal reflex.
back:
• Triggers: Distention or irritation of the cecum.
• Consequences: Inhibits ileal peristalsis and intensifies ileocecal sphincter contraction to prevent backflow and slow emptying.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: The vagovagal reflex that allows the stomach to reduce its muscular tone to accommodate up to 1.5 liters of food is known as [___].
back:
• Receptive Relaxation
• Pathway: From stomach to brain stem and back via vagus nerves.
• Purpose: Maintains low intragastric pressure during food storage.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: A patient with acute peritonitis presents with a silent abdomen and lack of bowel movements. Which reflex is responsible for this generalized GI inhibition?
back:
• Peritoneointestinal reflex
• Trigger: Irritation of the peritoneum.
• Effect: Strongly inhibits excitatory enteric nerves, causing intestinal paralysis.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: How do reflexes integrated entirely within the enteric nervous system (ENS) regulate local segment function?
back:
• Mechanism: Local sensory neurons detect tactile/chemical stimuli.
• Functions: Control local secretion, peristalsis, mixing contractions, and local inhibitory effects without extrinsic involvement.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Distinguish between the gastroileal reflex and the enterogastric reflex in terms of their effect on motility.
back:
• Gastroileal: Excitatory; stomach distention intensifies ileal peristalsis to force chyme through the ileocecal valve.
• Enterogastric: Inhibitory; duodenal distention slows gastric emptying.

category: Enlist the gastrointestinal reflexes & explain the functions of these reflexes
front: Identify the non-GI organ-originated reflexes that inhibit intestinal activity in response to visceral irritation.
back:
• Renointestinal reflex (kidney irritation).
• Vesicointestinal reflex (bladder irritation).
• Both inhibit intestinal motility to prioritize the primary pathology.

category: Enlist the hormones acting on GIT, their stimuli, site of release and actions
front: The primary hormone responsible for stimulating gastric acid secretion and the growth of the gastric mucosa is secreted by [___] cells of the antrum.
back:
• **G cells**
• Stimuli: Gastric distention, protein products, and Gastrin-Releasing Peptide (GRP)
• Action: Potent stimulation of parietal cell HCl secretion.

category: Enlist the hormones acting on GIT, their stimuli, site of release and actions
front: A 40-year-old female experiences RUQ pain after a fatty meal. This pain is triggered by gallbladder contraction mediated by a hormone released from [___] cells.
back:
• **I cells** (Duodenum/Jejunum)
• Hormone: **Cholecystokinin (CCK)**
• Mechanism: Contracts gallbladder and relaxes Sphincter of Oddi while inhibiting gastric emptying.

category: Enlist the hormones acting on GIT, their stimuli, site of release and actions
front: Explain the mechanism by which Secretin facilitates the neutralization of acidic gastric juice in the duodenum.
back:
• Stimulus: Acidic chyme (pH <4.5) entering duodenum
• Release Site: **S cells** (Duodenum)
• Action: Stimulates pancreatic and biliary ductal cells to secrete large volumes of bicarbonate-rich fluid.

category: Enlist the hormones acting on GIT, their stimuli, site of release and actions
front: A patient with a suspected gastrinoma presents with severe peptic ulcers. Contrast the physiological effect of Gastrin on the gastric mucosa with the effect of Secretin.
back:
• **Gastrin**: Stimulates mucosal growth (trophic effect) and acid secretion.
• **Secretin**: Inhibits Gastrin release and gastric acid secretion; protects mucosa via bicarbonate.

category: Enlist the hormones acting on GIT, their stimuli, site of release and actions
front: Describe the 'Incretin' effect of Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Peptide (GIP) on the pancreas.
back:
• Stimulus: Protein, fat, and carbohydrates in the upper small intestine
